title: Cook for the judge, stay yourself
allegory: RLHF is a chef learning to cook for a judge who stands in for the town's taste: each dish is built one ingredient at a time and scored only when it is served, and every choice their frozen twin (the chef as they were before training) would never have made costs a fine.
map: the chef, adding one ingredient at a time
the policy π_θ: the state is the whole sequence so far, the action is the next token
the judge, trained on which of two dishes diners preferred
a reward model fitted to human rankings (InstructGPT); ARENA swaps in a hand-written reward: count the full stops
a score only when the dish is served
reward r_T = R(s_T) on the final token, zero on every token before it
the chef's hunch, mid-cook, about how the dish will score
the value head: a scalar critic reading the residual stream, sharing the policy's trunk
a fine for straying from the frozen twin's cooking
− kl_coef · KL(π_θ ‖ π_ref), where π_ref is a frozen copy of the base model; kl_coef = 2.5 in ARENA
where_else: GRPO: the same loop with the value head removed; the group's mean score plays the critic's role
Christiano et al. (2017), the ancestor: people picked which of two clips looked more like a backflip, and a reward predictor learned from those picks
Any optimiser chasing a measurable stand-in for what you really want, where something has to stop it wandering off into nonsense that scores well
A Bayesian update: old odds reweighted by evidence is the same shape as the tuned model's odds, the frozen twin's odds tilted by the score

hamming.what: Reinforcement learning on a language model: each next token is an action, a reward model trained on human preference rankings scores the finished text, and a KL penalty keeps the tuned model near a frozen copy of itself.
hamming.when: After pretraining, as the finishing step that turns a text predictor into an assistant, and whenever you can score whole outputs but cannot write down the right answer token by token.
hamming.why: It made 'follows instructions' something you could optimise rather than hope for: labellers preferred the 1.3B InstructGPT to the 175B GPT-3 it came from, a model a hundred times larger.

object.title: The three shelves
object.subtitle: Where a tuned model settles between the judge and its frozen twin, for any strength of the fine

cap.1: Back shelf: how many full stops each ending has, all this judge cares about. Middle: the frozen twin's odds. Front: the model being tuned.
cap.2: Back row is ARENA's toy reward (count the full stops). Middle row is π_ref, a frozen copy of the base model. Front row is where the tuned policy settles for this kl_coef. At 10 the fine is heavy, so the front copies the middle.
cap.3: The front row is the optimum of E[R] − β·KL(π ‖ π_ref): π_ref(y)·exp(R(y)/β), normalised. It is an idealised end point, not a finite PPO run, and the twin's odds here are made up for illustration.

cap.1: ARENA's default fine, kl_coef = 2.5. The front row leans toward the full stops, but plain 'ran home' is still its likeliest ending.
cap.2: At kl_coef = 2.5 the tilt is exp(R / 2.5): each extra full stop multiplies an ending's odds by about 1.5 before normalising. Rare endings stay fairly rare because the twin gave them small odds to start with.
cap.3: By the chain rule, per-token KLs add up to the KL between whole sequences, so tilting whole endings is a fair picture of what a per-token penalty targets. The small entropy bonus (ent_coef = 0.001) barely shifts it.

cap.1: Loosen the fine to 1. Now 'Yes. No. Ok.' and '......' hold most of the odds. The twin's taste is losing the argument.
cap.2: Each full stop now multiplies the odds by e ≈ 2.7. The six-stop ending started at 1% and now leads. The reward is climbing; ask whether the text is still something anyone wants to read.
cap.3: Smaller β lets the reward term outweigh the KL term, so the settled policy's distance from π_ref grows quickly as β falls. That trade is what the W10 demo, The Overoptimisation Curve, lets you explore.

cap.1: Almost no fine: '......' takes nearly everything. That is mode collapse. The model stops being a language model and just prints full stops.
cap.2: ARENA's warning case: kl_coef left at 0.0 after the plumbing test, plus a reward that counts characters. The samples turn into endless full stops while the reward curve looks lovely.
cap.3: As β → 0 the optimum becomes a point mass on argmax R. The case study's diagnosis: once mass concentrates, an entropy bonus at ent_coef = 0.001 is far too weak to spread it back out.

cap.1: The frozen twin is why a tuned assistant still sounds like language. Steering with RLHF means choosing what the judge rewards and how hard the fine pulls.
cap.2: The case study's fixes: check kl_coef is back on (2.5), fix the reward (count tokens that contain a full stop, or normalise by length), and log sample completions every phase, never the curve alone.
cap.3: InstructGPT (Ouyang et al., 2022) fitted R to human rankings instead of counting characters, but the shape of the problem is the same: β sets how far the policy may travel from π_ref to chase R.

predict.q: Slide kl_coef toward 0. What does the front row turn into?

options.t: A copy of the frozen twin's row
One tall bar on '......', the judge's favourite

predict.why: With no fine for drifting, the best policy puts everything on the top-scoring ending. That is the mode collapse ARENA's full-stop reward is designed to show you.

predict.q: Which row never changes while the model trains?
predict.why: π_ref is a frozen copy of the base model; only the policy and its value head get updates. A fixed anchor is what lets the KL penalty measure drift at all.

predict.q: Mean reward climbs smoothly and never stops. What do you check first?

options.t: That kl_coef is back on after the kl_coef = 0.0 plumbing test
That the learning rate is high enough
Nothing: rising reward means it is working

predict.why: The case study names the switched-off penalty from the plumbing test as the single most common cause. Then fix the reward, and read sample completions next to the curve.

object.where: Old odds times exp(score / β) is the shape of a Bayesian update: a prior reweighted by evidence, here the frozen twin reweighted by the judge.
